meta.ogDescription: Genuine Marie Curie: a letter of November 25, 1888 to her cousin Henrietta, printed in Eve Curie's Madame Curie (1937). Quote sites rarely give the source.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Marie wrote it in a letter to her cousin Henrietta dated November 25, 1888, while she was working as a governess at Szczuki. The letter is printed in Eve Curie’s Madame Curie: A Biography (1937), translated by Vincent Sheean. The popular wording matches that English translation word for word.

source.heading: The documented source

source.excerpt: I was barely eighteen when I came here, and what have I not been through! There have been moments which I shall certainly count among the most cruel of my life … I feel everything very violently, with a physical violence, and then I give myself a shaking, the vigor of my nature conquers, and it seems to me that I am coming out of a nightmare. … First principle: never to let one’s self be beaten down by persons or by events.
trail: Wikiquote does not list the line on its main page. It appears only on the Talk:Marie Curie “Unsourced” list ↗, among quotes still waiting for a source.
Quote Investigator has no article on it. A site search for “beaten down by persons” ↗ returns “Nothing Found.”
The scanned full text of Eve Curie’s Madame Curie (1937) ↗ prints the exact sentence in “Manya to Henrietta, November 25, 1888,” in Chapter VI.
The line is not in Marie Curie’s own Pierre Curie with Autobiographical Notes (1923) ↗, so the biography’s letter is where the line actually comes from.
source.excerptNote: From Vincent Sheean’s 1937 English translation of Eve Curie’s biography. The ellipses are in the printed text. The circulating version keeps only the final sentence.

author.name: Marie Curie
author.heading: About Marie Curie
author.bio: Marie Curie was born Maria Skłodowska in Warsaw. She pioneered the study of radioactivity, was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize, and remains the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences. As a young woman she worked from 1886 to 1889 as a governess at Szczuki, and this line comes from a letter she wrote there.

misattribution.heading: Real line, missing source
misattribution.intro: Curie is a magnet for invented quotes, but this one is genuine. The problem is that it travels without any source attached.

items.why: Goalcast’s Curie list ↗ prints the sentence word for word but names no letter, date or book. That leaves readers no way to check it.
Wikiquote keeps the line on its Talk page “Unsourced” list ↗ and not on the Marie Curie page itself. Without the 1888 letter, it can look like one more unverified Curie quote.

misattribution.truthLine: The sentence comes from Marie’s letter to her cousin Henrietta of November 25, 1888, as printed in Eve Curie’s Madame Curie (1937), translated by Vincent Sheean ↗.

context.heading: A governess’s private resolve
lead: This is not a public motto. It closes a frank passage in a private letter. Marie wrote it while she was working as a governess at Szczuki, and in the letter she calls her life there like that of “one of those slugs which haunt the dirty water of our river.” She tells her cousin that some moments there were “among the most cruel of my life,” then describes shaking herself out of it.

Her daughter Eve printed the letter in her 1937 biography. Through Vincent Sheean’s English translation, this one sentence became a stand-alone inspirational quote. Removed from its letter, it lost the date and the person it was written to.
context.pull: the vigor of my nature conquers, and it seems to me that I am coming out of a nightmare
